name: Andalusian Spanish Revival

revival_periods.note: Sustained revival in Santa Barbara, Montecito, and coastal Southern California, supported by design review boards that still require it.

lineage.note: The claimed ancestor, and unusually well studied for a revival: Californian architects travelled to southern Spain and published measured photographs of ordinary farm buildings rather than monuments.
Tilework, courtyard water features, and geometric surface ornament quoted at second hand.
Californian architects had the hacienda in front of them and Andalusia only in books and on summer trips; the built result blends both.
The actual professional lineage. George Washington Smith, Reginald Johnson, and Wallace Neff composed in a Beaux-Arts manner and dressed the result in whitewashed lime.

description.short: The rural, whitewashed, deliberately plain branch of Spanish Colonial Revival, taken from Andalusian farmhouses rather than from Spanish churches, and centred on Santa Barbara in the 1920s.
description.long:
Spanish Colonial Revival at large had a taste for magnificence — carved Churrigueresque portals, twisted columns, ornamental ironwork, the whole retable façade brought down to domestic scale. The Andalusian branch is the reaction against that within the same style, and it is one of the more disciplined acts of restraint in American revival architecture. Its practitioners had noticed that the buildings they actually admired in southern Spain were not the cathedrals but the farms: white lime-washed masses, almost no ornament, tile roofs of a single low pitch, a few small deep-set windows, and a wooden gate opening into a courtyard where all the pleasure of the place was kept.

George Washington Smith is the central figure, and his conversion is instructive. He trained as an architect, went to Paris to become a painter, and came back to build in Montecito a house of such plainness that clients began asking for one like it. What he had understood is that the Andalusian effect depends on subtraction: the power of a whitewashed wall comes from its being uninterrupted, and every additional window, vent, or decorative bracket spends some of it. The 1925 Santa Barbara earthquake, which levelled much of the downtown and prompted the city to rebuild under an architectural review board committed to this idiom, gave the manner a whole city to work on.

Standing before one of these houses, the first thing you register is mass and the second is shadow. There is very little to look at — a plane of lime plaster, a low red-brown roof line, a dark rectangle of opening set back six or eight inches into the wall, a black iron grille. The building withholds. Then a door in a wall opens and the withheld thing is behind it: a court, a fountain or a runnel, tile, shade, a wall of jasmine, and rooms arranged around the court in a single-room-deep range so that every one of them is lit and ventilated from two sides. The sequence is the architecture. The elevation is merely the wall that makes the sequence possible.

Of everything in this taxonomy, this variant has the strongest technical claim on the American Sun Belt today. Its climate logic is exact and it is a logic almost nothing in current production housing uses: thermal mass, minimized and shaded glazing, deep reveals, courtyard microclimate, single-pile ranges for cross ventilation. The idiom is usually sold on romance. It should be sold on physics.

defining_characteristics: Uninterrupted planes of white or cream lime-washed stucco with softened, hand-troweled arrises
Ornament almost wholly absent from the wall, concentrated at a single door, gate, or window grille
Low-pitched clay barrel-tile roof, 3:12 to 5:12, with minimal or no eave overhang and no gutter expressed
Openings small relative to wall area, deeply recessed, and irregularly placed according to interior need rather than facade rhythm
A courtyard or walled garden carrying the principal outdoor life of the house, entered through a controlled gate
Single-pile ranges of rooms wrapping the court, lit and ventilated from two sides
Wrought iron used sparingly and structurally — grilles, gate hardware, a balcony rail — never as applied decoration
diagnostic_tells: Window reveals deep enough to throw a hard shadow at midday — 8 to 14 inches, expressing wall mass
Asymmetrical, apparently accidental fenestration on a formally composed plan
No visible gutters, no fascia board, tile running directly to a plastered edge
A single ornamental event on an otherwise silent elevation
Wall planes meeting at slightly rounded, imperfect corners rather than crisp arrises

distinguished_from.difference: The parent style permits and often features elaborate carved Churrigueresque entries, twisted columns, applied ornament, and a symmetrical show facade. The Andalusian branch systematically refuses all of it and takes its precedent from farm buildings rather than from churches and civic monuments.

Mission Revival is earlier (c. 1890–1920), thinner in wall, and defined by the curvilinear parapet, the arcaded corridor, and a quatrefoil or espadaña quotation from the California mission churches. Andalusian Revival has no curvilinear parapet, expresses far greater wall mass, and refers to Spain directly rather than to California's own Spanish past.

Mediterranean Revival is larger, more symmetrical, more Italianate in its classical detail, and typically has a formal frontal composition with a centred entry. Andalusian Revival is smaller-scaled, asymmetrical, and organizes itself around a court rather than around a facade.

proportional_system.governing_logic: No classical module. Governed by wall mass, opening-to-wall ratio, and the proportion of the courtyard to the height of the ranges enclosing it.
typical_ratios: Glazing 8%-18% of wall area on sun-exposed elevations
Reveal depth 8"-14", not less than one-third the apparent wall thickness
Courtyard width at least 1.5x the height of the tallest enclosing range, so winter sun reaches the floor at 34 degrees latitude
Roof pitch 3:12 to 5:12, constant across the composition
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Irregular and interior-driven; openings are placed by the room behind them, and the elevation is composed by the balance of solid to void rather than by a repeating bay.

massing_affinities.note: The accretive farm cluster reads correctly if the ridge heights step.
A symmetrical double-pile block with a centred entry contradicts the type at the level of plan.

constraints.statement: Window reveal depth not less than 8 inches. A flush window in a stucco wall destroys the expression of mass on which the entire idiom depends, and is the single most common failure in contemporary versions.
Not more than one elaborated ornamental event per elevation — a carved surround, a tiled stair, an iron balcony. Two or more and the composition becomes the parent style, not this variant.
Glazing on south and west elevations not to exceed 18% of wall area unless shaded by an arcade or deep overhang of not less than 4 feet.

test.note: Tests the 18% glazing cap. The shading exception (unshaded, or shaded by an arcade or an overhang of not less than 4 feet) is a conditional escape clause with no vocabulary support for combining a percentage test with an alternate-compliance-path and stays prose.

constraints.statement: Roof pitch 3:12 to 5:12 with barrel or two-piece mission tile; eave overhang 0 to 12 inches, terminating in a plastered edge or a shaped rafter tail. Composition shingle and a fascia-and-gutter edge void the type.

test.note: Tests the roof pitch range. Eave overhang (0-12in) and the required barrel/two-piece mission tile roofing material are the statement's other clauses and stay prose.

constraints.statement: The courtyard must be reachable only through a controlled gate or zaguan, and must be enclosed on at least three sides. A patio open to the street is a different building.

exemplars.name: Casa del Herrero
exemplars.note: George Washington Smith, with gardens by Ralph Stevens and Lockwood de Forest; among the most intact Andalusian-mode houses in the United States, and a National Historic Landmark.
exemplars.why: The Casa del Herrero foundation's own words -- 'one of the finest standing examples of Spanish Colonial Revival Architecture in America' -- and the National Historic Landmark designation of 2009. It is the foundation's own page, and not the designation, that ties the two together: it says the house 'maintains National Historic Landmark status, partly due to its eclectic mix of Country Place Era and Moorish-inspired gardens'.

exemplars.name: Santa Barbara County Courthouse
exemplars.note: William Mooser III. Civic rather than domestic, and more elaborate than the domestic mode, but the building that fixed the city's post-earthquake idiom.
exemplars.why: It is the building Santa Barbara's own post-earthquake idiom is measured against, which is a claim about one city rather than about the Andalusian mode wherever it went -- the node's own exemplar note already says it is civic and more elaborate than the domestic case.

exemplars.name: Jackling House
exemplars.note: George Washington Smith. Demolished in 2011; documented photographically and worth citing as evidence rather than as a visitable building.
exemplars.why: Demolished in 2011 and surviving only in photographs and the periodical record the Pacific Coast Architecture Database lists, so it can be read as evidence and never visited or measured.

exemplars.name: Heberton House
exemplars.note: George Washington Smith's own first house, built after his move from Paris in 1916 and, in the UCSB archive's words, 'designed to resemble the Spanish farmhouses he had seen in Europe'. Published as La Casa Dracaena in Architectural Record in October 1920, and as Craig Heberton's house in the Western Architect of 1922 -- the sources disagree about both the date and the client and the precedent record carries both.
exemplars.why: The University of California Santa Barbara's Architecture and Design Collection, which holds Smith's drawings, credits this house with bringing him 'national attention' in 1920 and with turning him from a painter into an architect -- the mode's starting point on its own archive's judgment.

exemplars.name: The Andalusia
exemplars.note: Arthur and Nina Zwebell, designed round a planted court. The Andalusian mode as rented urban housing rather than as a country house, and the reason it reached a city rather than a hillside; National Register-listed in 2003 and a Los Angeles Historic-Cultural Monument since 1989.
exemplars.why: National Register-listed on its own merits rather than as part of a district, with the encyclopaedia's own description naming the material set -- exposed and cantilevered beams, wrought iron, terracotta tile, buff stucco -- which makes it a type specimen for the courtyard case.

exemplars.name: Lobero Theatre
exemplars.location: 33 East Canon Perdido Street, Santa Barbara, California
exemplars.note: George Washington Smith with Lutah Maria Riggs, opened August 1924 on the site of the 1873 opera house. The mode on a public street a year before the earthquake, and the encyclopaedia ties its reopening to the city's first Old Spanish Days Fiesta and to 'the city's emerging Spanish Colonial Revival identity'.
exemplars.why: A California Historical Landmark that matters as the moment Santa Barbara adopted the manner publicly, which is a fact about that city and that year rather than about the domestic mode wherever it was built.

sources: McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses
Gebhard, George Washington Smith, 1876-1930: The Spanish Colonial Revival in California
Byne and Stapley, Spanish Architecture of the Sixteenth Century and Provincial Houses in Spain
Baer, The Architecture of Wallace Neff
Gellner, Storybook Style and Casa California (Winter)

proportion_packs.note: This style's own governing_logic is explicitly non-classical ('No classical module. Governed by wall mass, opening-to-wall ratio, and the proportion of the courtyard') and its symmetry is recorded as 'balanced-asymmetrical' -- the same species of composition facade-picturesque was built to check. Bind only the pack's general compositional invariants: the dominance rule (one mass must clearly outrank the others), the lever-arm/moment rule for balancing a subordinate wing or gate against the main range, the two-continuous-datum rule, and the window-proportion-count and window-grouping rules (2-3 opening proportions at most, adjacent groups differing in count) -- all of which read as a formal restatement, in a different vocabulary, of this style's own c02 constraint (not more than one elaborated ornamental event per elevation) and its 'irregular and interior-driven' bay rhythm. Do NOT apply the pack's datum_stack assembly -- water table as an exposed 'rubble, boulder, brick or shingled skirt', a clapboard-to-shingle material change at the second-floor sill -- because that stack is calibrated to wood-frame, shingled and clapboarded Anglo-American construction and describes nothing about a continuous lime-washed stucco mass with hand-troweled, deliberately imperfect arrises. The style's own real governing numbers -- reveal depth 8-14in, glazing capped at 18% of sun-exposed wall -- are not modeled by this or any pack in the corpus.

The refusal branch, and it is bound rather than refused because its rule is this pack's rule with a smaller number in it: 'not more than one elaborated ornamental event per elevation -- two or more and the composition becomes the parent style, not this variant.' The variant is defined against `spanish-colonial-revival` entirely by the count, which is the clearest demonstration in the corpus of why `event_count` had to be a rule rather than a remark. Bound for the rationing rules alone; this branch takes its precedent from farm buildings and has no retablo to proportion.

Bound for the daylight-depth rule alone, which the pack itself calls 'physics rather than custom... true in 1650, true now.' This style's defining single-pile ranges 'wrapping the court, lit and ventilated from two sides' are exactly the condition the rule describes (max depth ~2 to 2.25x window head height from one window wall), doubled by having a window wall on each side; the style's own courtyard-width rule (>=1.5x the height of the tallest enclosing range, so winter sun reaches the floor at 34 degrees latitude) is the same kind of physically-derived constraint the pack specializes in, applied to the court instead of the room. Do not carry over the pack's hearth-reach or joist-span derivations, or its room-count-from-frontage arithmetic -- this is a masonry/stucco courtyard house with no chimney-count logic and no timber bay to tile against.

Secondary, not primary: the revival composes picturesquely (facade-picturesque is already bound as its facade pack) and reaches for the Moorish arch as vocabulary rather than as the system the whole building is generated from. Binding it primary would claim a geometric discipline the revival does not actually keep.

declined_packs.reason: The pack's own notes present it as a classical order-system and nothing else -- a column of twenty modules carrying an entablature of a quarter its height divided 3:3:4 -- and the two slots it actually governs on this node are derived straight off that module: an envelope cornice of storey_height/4 * (4/10) carrying a dentil course, and an envelope frieze the pack says Vignola 'expected to be richly carved'. The node's governing_logic opens by refusing exactly that authority, and its defining characteristics put a 'Low-pitched clay barrel-tile roof, 3:12 to 5:12, with minimal or no eave overhang and no gutter expressed' precisely where the dentil cornice would have to run, with 'Ornament almost wholly absent from the wall' where the carved frieze would sit. This is not the blanket sentence applied blindly to any pack: the pack's own stated subject IS a classical module, so the node's sentence meets it head-on rather than glancing off it. The Beaux-Arts lineage edge does not rescue it -- that note says the architects 'composed in a Beaux-Arts manner and dressed the result in whitewashed lime', locating the classicism in the plan and the lime on the elevation.
declined_packs.quote: No classical module. Governed by wall mass, opening-to-wall ratio, and the proportion of the courtyard to the height of the ranges enclosing it.
declined_packs.note: Governs 2 slots (cornice, frieze). Declining hands both to palladio-tuscan (italian-renaissance); 0 slots lose all dimensioning. Worth stating plainly: the node still ends up dimensioned by a classical order, so this decline does not make the style non-classical -- it stops the most ornate of the five orders from setting the eave of the style's plainest branch, and leaves the plainest order in its place.

declined_packs.reason: The pack's own skeleton note states its subject plainly as a classical order-system and nothing else -- a column of twenty modules carrying a five-module entablature divided 3:3:4, Vignola's own figures from the Regola -- so every dimension it offers is a multiple of a classical module. The node's governing_logic opens by refusing exactly that authority and names what governs instead: wall mass, opening-to-wall ratio, and the court-to-range proportion. This is not the blanket sentence glancing off an unrelated pack; the pack IS a module system, so the node's sentence meets it head-on, in the same way the node's own already-recorded decline of vignola-composite does. The Corinthian case is if anything sharper: the node's defining characteristics put 'Ornament almost wholly absent from the wall' and a barrel-tile roof with 'minimal or no eave overhang and no gutter expressed' precisely where a Corinthian entablature and its carved frieze would have to run, and the Beaux-Arts lineage edge locates that training in the plan while the elevation is whitewashed lime.
declined_packs.quote: No classical module. Governed by wall mass, opening-to-wall ratio, and the proportion of the courtyard to the height of the ranges enclosing it.
declined_packs.note: Measured --impact: the pack reaches this node from beaux-arts-french at cascade depth 6 with no direct lineage edge, and it currently governs 0 slots (it is outranked at every address it could reach). Declining it changes no dimension on this node and no slot loses any dimensioning; the effect is on the meter and on the record of what this style refuses. --pair reports no live gate.
